question: According to Table 2.1, report the values across all four income groups (Low-income, Lower-middle-income, Upper-middle-income, High-income) for all five openness indicators, and calculate the percentage-point gap between High-income and Low-income countries for 'Available in machine readable format (%)'.
answer:
According to Table 2.1, the values for the five openness indicators across income groups are as follows:

- Openness score (0–100): Low-income (38), Lower-middle-income (47), Upper-middle-income (50), High-income (66).
- Available in machine readable format (%): Low-income (37), Lower-middle-income (51), Upper-middle-income (61), High-income (81).
- Available in nonproprietary format (%): Low-income (75), Lower-middle-income (85), Upper-middle-income (81), High-income (84).
- Download options available (%): Low-income (56), Lower-middle-income (68), Upper-middle-income (68), High-income (78).
- Open terms of use/license (%): Low-income (11), Lower-middle-income (19), Upper-middle-income (22), High-income (44).

The percentage-point gap between High-income (81%) and Low-income (37%) countries for 'Available in machine readable format (%)' is 44 percentage points [wdr2021:p83:vis_table_2_1].

question: List all seven research areas in Table 4.1 ('Selected research gaps to be addressed to advance the use of private intent data for development'), and explain why footnote b uses the term 'deidentification' instead of 'anonymization'.
answer: The seven research areas listed in Table 4.1 are: Societal impacts, Quality standards, External validity, Machine learning, Training and validation data, Deidentification, and Capturing longitudinal change [wdr2021:p162:vis_table_4_1]. The term 'deidentification' is used instead of 'anonymization' because, although data are processed to deidentify individuals, these data may become identifiable in the future as computing and machine learning advance, meaning data may never be truly anonymized [wdr2021:p162:vis_table_4_1, wdr2021:p162:p6]. [wdr2021:p162:p6]

Table 4.1 Selected research gaps to be addressed to advance the use of private intent data for
development
Research area | Examples of research gaps
Societal impacts | • | How do we ensure that algorithmic-based policy making can lead to fair outcomes?
• | How can we increase the transparency and interpretability of policy predictions using private intent
data?
• | How can we design algorithms that can be safeguarded against manipulation?
• | What are the trade-offs between granularity and precision, and what is the optimal mix for
targeting of development programs?
Quality standards | • | How can standards be created, agreed on, updated, and communicated to the general
development community? Who needs to be part of these conversations?
• | To ensure that policy makers can trust and use results, what should the standards be for accuracy
and precision for frontier applications that use private intent data or that combine public intent and
private intent data?
External validitya | • | How promising is the approach of building models in countries that have data and applying them
to countries with limited data?
• | How can issues akin to data profiling and discrimination be avoided when using pre-trained
models from higher-income countries in cases of novel development use?
• | To what extent can applications that combine public intent survey data with private intent data
predict values calculated from census data within a country?
Machine learning | • | How does the approach to machine learning and spatial feature selection need to change from
common machine learning tasks to more specialized tasks that will aid development policy?
• | Which features best predict spatial variation in development outcomes in different contexts? What
are the trade-offs between predictive accuracy and cost?
Training and validation data | • | What should be the required volume of and approach to public intent data collection for calibrating
and validating machine learning algorithms that combine public intent and private intent data?
Deidentificationb | • | How do deidentification methods need to change to protect individuals and companies when
private intent data are used for public benefit?
• | How does (spatial) deidentification of public intent data affect the accuracy and precision of
applications that use public intent data to calibrate and validate machine learning algorithms that
combine public intent and private intent data?
Capturing longitudinal | • | How do accuracy and precision differ in applications that aim to estimate longitudinal change
change | versus obtaining cross-sectional predictions for the same development outcome?
• | What features best predict longitudinal change in different contexts?
• | How can we ensure the stability over time of algorithms aimed at predicting changes in policy
outcomes?
• | When public intent survey data are combined with imagery—specifically, spatial features
(predictors) extracted via deep-learning techniques—in order to derive high-resolution estimates of
a development outcome, how do the spatial, spectral,c and temporal resolution of satellite imagery
affect the accuracy and precision of the predictions for the outcome of interest?
• | Do these effects vary based on the decisions on the size of satellite imagery grids that are
processed for extracting spatial features?
a.  External validity relates to the research findings of one location holding true in another location.
b.  The term deidentification is used instead of anonymization because, although data are processed to deidentify any individual, these data may become identifiable in the future as computing and
machine learning advance. Thus data may never be truly anonymized.
c. | “Spectral” refers to different wavelengths on the visual spectrum. Satellite images typically have multiple “bands” that capture different spectral ranges.

Investing in research
Investments in research are needed to develop
methods and enable lower-income countries to
grow research programs that leverage private intent
data for public policy. The research community can
achieve quick wins by focusing on foundational
areas such as testing whether validated methods
in one region translate to contexts where data are
sparse. Over the longer term, research strategies
would benefit from building validation and training
datasets in lower-income countries to avoid issues
similar to data profiling and discrimination when
using pre-trained models from higher-income countries. The selections that follow describe some of the
high-priority research needed to advance the use of
private intent data for public benefit in the short and
long term.

question: According to Table 5.1, compare the sequenced data infrastructure recommendations for 'Connecting people' versus 'Connecting countries' across all three country maturity stages.
answer:
According to Table 5.1, the sequenced data infrastructure recommendations for 'Connecting people' and 'Connecting countries' across the three maturity stages are as follows: 

1. **Establishing fundamentals**: For 'Connecting people,' the recommendation is to eliminate coverage gaps by reducing costs through wholesale and retail competition, infrastructure sharing, and well-crafted state support. For 'Connecting countries,' the recommendation is to ensure adequate international bandwidth and create a competitive market environment for international gateways and internet service providers [wdr2021:p197:vis_table_5_1].

2. **Initiating data flows**: For 'Connecting people,' the recommendation is to narrow usage gaps through digital literacy campaigns, basic education investment, lower taxation/import duties on low-end handsets, and support for local handset manufacturing ventures. For 'Connecting countries,' the recommendation is to encourage the creation of the first domestic internet exchange point (IXP), facilitate participation by all relevant domestic players, allow additional IXPs to emerge and mature, and encourage arrangements to cache popular international internet content on local servers [wdr2021:p197:vis_table_5_1].

3. **Optimizing the system**: For 'Connecting people,' the recommendation is to upgrade digital networks to the latest generation to improve speed, efficiency, and consumption. For 'Connecting countries,' the recommendation is to create a supportive environment where colocation data centers can emerge, integrate with IXPs, and provide on-ramp access to cloud services [wdr2021:p197:vis_table_5_1].

results.text:
There is no singular blueprint for how to build
an INDS. It certainly must be funded sufficiently to
implement the infrastructure and institutions necessary for the system to function well. Incentives need
to be in place to produce, protect, and share data,
and to create a data culture in which people demand
transparency and accountability. But how countries
move toward this vision of an INDS will depend on
their current capacity and the parameters of the social
contract for data. Although the path toward an INDS
will differ for each country, this Report proposes a
sequenced maturity model to help assess progress
and identify areas for more attention to further the
development of a well-functioning INDS.

answer:
Based on Table 6.1, the average regulatory scores (0–100) for the requested groups across the Safeguards and Enablers sub-indicators are as follows: 

For High-income countries: Safeguards (Cybersecurity and cybercrime: 73, Personal data: 59, Nonpersonal data: 43) and Enablers (E-commerce and e-transactions: 86, Public intent data: 69, Private intent data: 30). 

For Low-income countries: Safeguards (Cybersecurity and cybercrime: 39, Personal data: 31, Nonpersonal data: 47) and Enablers (E-commerce and e-transactions: 59, Public intent data: 28, Private intent data: 3). 

For the Global group: Safeguards (Cybersecurity and cybercrime: 56, Personal data: 44, Nonpersonal data: 38) and Enablers (E-commerce and e-transactions: 73, Public intent data: 50, Private intent data: 17). [wdr2021:p227:vis_table_6_1]

results.text:
Development is at an intermediate level in areas
such as enabling reuse of public intent data, safeguarding both personal and nonpersonal data, protecting cybersecurity, and combating cybercrime. By
far the weakest area of performance of the surveyed
countries is enablers for private intent data. Overall,
the average scores of high-income countries are not
very high in absolute terms, warranting an advanced
(green) classification in table 6.1 in only one case. And
the score differential between high- and low-income
countries is relatively small (rarely more than 30
points). Both findings indicate the novel challenges
of developing a sound data governance legal framework and the significant progress all countries need
to make.

results.text:
Although the discussion
here deals mainly with domestic data transactions,
many of the enablers can be adapted to cross-border
data transactions (see chapter 7).
Across the 80 countries surveyed for this Report,
just under half (47 percent) of the elements of a
good-practice regulatory framework for enabling
data use and reuse are in place. The scores range
considerably, from 30 percent among low-income
countries to 62 percent among high-income countries. Although Estonia and the United Kingdom
stand out among the high-income countries surveyed
for the most advanced enablers, their performance
is matched in the middle-income group by Mexico.

results.text:
Stronger restrictions on cross-border data flows,
such as those found in the limited transfers model,
can be particularly detrimental to international
trade. Because trade in services relies on the global
movement of data, including personal data, regulations that require the maintenance or processing of
data within a country or a particular region can be a
costly impediment. Restrictive data policies—especially mandatory localization requirements—reduce
imports of data-intensive services in the countries
imposing them, which, in turn, limits cross-border
digital trade flows.

results.text:
Data intermediation and
collaboration
Another way to enable better data use, reuse, and
sharing is through data intermediation. An entity
(data intermediary) or simply a contractual arrangement facilitates the collection, validation, and aggregation of data from data contributors and makes data
understandable, usable, and accessible to data users.52
Data intermediaries can facilitate data sharing in a
trusted, more efficient manner between government
institutions or between government and nongovernment actors as part of the broader national data
system (table 8.3).
Data intermediaries (sometimes called infomediaries) can be important enablers in low- and middle-
income economies that may have gaps in their
data management frameworks or weak enforcement.

Data intermediation for public or common goods. New
types of intermediaries oriented toward public or
common goods are emerging. Data collaboratives
facilitate and promote data sharing between diverse
actors by ensuring compliance with minimum data
protection and security rules, as well as quality standards and rules to make data interoperable.
Data collaboratives can involve a diverse array
of actors—such as government institutions, private
companies, research institutions, or CSOs—that come
together to exchange data with a view toward solving public problems. 59 Data sharing arrangements 60
could, but need not, involve the creation of a separate
entity tasked with managing data, including ensuring safe and ethical usage.

question: According to the theory of change diagram in Figure O.1 (PDF page 24), which three main channels generate/use data, what positive outcomes vs negative risks appear on the right-hand side, and what do the two-way 'Reuse' arrows represent?
answer: According to Figure O.1, the three main channels (stakeholder groups) that generate and use data are: 1) Individuals, civil society, and academia; 2) Government and international organizations; and 3) The private sector [wdr2021:p24:vis_figure_o_1]. The positive outcomes (shown in green) include greater transparency, greater accountability, better policy making and service delivery, and increased business opportunities [wdr2021:p24:vis_figure_o_1]. The negative risks (shown in red) include criminal activity/dark net, political surveillance, market concentration, widening inequality, and discrimination [wdr2021:p24:vis_figure_o_1]. The two-way 'Reuse' arrows represent the exchange and repurposing of data between these parties: the arrow between the private sector and government/international organizations indicates the reuse of data originally collected for commercial purposes for public policy (and vice versa); the arrow between individuals/civil society/academia and government/international organizations indicates data being exchanged and reused by those parties; and the final arrows reflect the use of private sector data by individuals/civil society/academia and the use of data/analysis generated by individuals/civil society/academia by firms [wdr2021:p24:vis_figure_o_1].

question: In Figure O.6 ('What happens in an integrated national data system?'), what are the five actions on data, five participant groups, four policy pillars, and foundational elements sustaining the system?
answer:
According to Figure O.6, an integrated national data system involves the following components: 

- Five actions on data: produced, protected, open, quality controlled, and used and reused [wdr2021:p37:vis_figure_o_6].
- Five participant groups: government entities, civil society and individuals, academic institutions, the private sector, and international organizations [wdr2021:p37:vis_figure_o_6].
- Four policy pillars: infrastructure, laws and regulations, economic policies, and institutions [wdr2021:p37:vis_figure_o_6].
- Foundational elements: human capital, data demand, trust, incentives, and funding [wdr2021:p37:vis_figure_o_6].

Foundations of an integrated national
data system
Putting these pillars in place for the national data
system is not easy. They need to be anchored in a
solid foundation of human capital, trust, funding,
incentives, and data demand. Trust in particular
plays a critical role in facilitating the integration of
participants and their data. It is essential to binding

Human capital. Human capital underpins
a well-functioning national data system.

question: According to Figure 3.1 ('The role of data in the production process: Pathways to development'), what two primary pathways lead from data in the production process, and what intermediate and final development outcomes result?
answer: According to Figure 3.1, the two primary pathways leading from data in the production process are 'Better data-driven decision-making' and 'Data-driven matching of demand and supply and transaction facilitation' [wdr2021:p114:vis_figure_3_1, wdr2021:p114:p0]. These pathways result in the following intermediate outcomes: 'Quality improvements', 'Cost reduction and process optimization', 'Product innovation', and 'intermediation and lower transaction costs' [wdr2021:p114:vis_figure_3_1, wdr2021:p114:p0]. The final development outcomes include: boosting opportunities for lagging regions and populations, creating new export opportunities, promoting productivity and growth, creating new markets and disrupting the market power of traditional incumbents, and supporting local entrepreneurship ecosystems [wdr2021:p114:vis_figure_3_1, wdr2021:p114:p0]. question: Based on the architecture diagram in Figure 5.1 ('The data infrastructure supply chain'), describe the three segments, their distance scales, their roles, and key facilities/technologies shown in each segment.
answer:
According to Figure 5.1, the data infrastructure supply chain consists of three segments: [wdr2021:p178:vis_figure_5_1]

1. **Cross-border network (international links):**
   - **Role:** Connects service centers to the worldwide internet.
   - **Typical distance:** >1,000 km.
   - **Key facilities/technologies:** Terrestrial fiber, WWW (internet), fiber, and subsea cables.

2. **Middle-mile network (distribution):**
   - **Role:** Connects bigger cities together and routes data to the service centers.
   - **Typical distance:** 10–1,000 km.
   - **Key facilities/technologies:** Fiber, fiber-optic backbone, fiber or microwave backbone, cellular towers, and satellite links.

3. **Last mile (access):**
   - **Role:** Distributes internet from the middle mile in the community to individual homes and businesses.
   - **Typical distance:** <1–5 km.
   - **Key facilities/technologies:** DSL, coaxial, wireless, Wi-Fi, LTE, TV white space, satellite link (DTH), wireless, and balloons and drones.

raw_action.query: Figure 5.1 The data infrastructure supply chain architecture diagram segments roles facilities technologies

raw_action.answer:
According to Figure 5.1, the data infrastructure supply chain consists of three segments: [wdr2021:p178:vis_figure_5_1]

1. **Cross-border network (international links):**
   - **Role:** Connects service centers to the worldwide internet.
   - **Typical distance:** >1,000 km.
   - **Key facilities/technologies:** Terrestrial fiber, WWW (internet), fiber, and subsea cables.

2. **Middle-mile network (distribution):**
   - **Role:** Connects bigger cities together and routes data to the service centers.
   - **Typical distance:** 10–1,000 km.
   - **Key facilities/technologies:** Fiber, fiber-optic backbone, fiber or microwave backbone, cellular towers, and satellite links.

3. **Last mile (access):**
   - **Role:** Distributes internet from the middle mile in the community to individual homes and businesses.
   - **Typical distance:** <1–5 km.
   - **Key facilities/technologies:** DSL, coaxial, wireless, Wi-Fi, LTE, TV white space, satellite link (DTH), wireless, and balloons and drones.

question: In Figure 9.3 ('Steps to integrating the public sector into the national data system'), what concrete steps are grouped under (1) Establishing fundamentals, (2) Initiating data flows, and (3) Optimizing the system?
answer:
In Figure 9.3, the steps to integrating the public sector into the national data system are grouped as follows: 

(1) Establishing fundamentals: 
- Policies: Recognize the importance of an integrated national data system in a high-level strategic document [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3, wdr2021:p330:p4]. 
- Laws and regulations: Put in place robust data protection regulations [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3, wdr2021:p330:p4]. 
- Human capital and funding: Strengthen the technical capacity and financing of NSOs [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3, wdr2021:p330:p4]. 
- Institutions: Create technical units in ministries to strengthen administrative data and coordinate data [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3, wdr2021:p330:p4]. 
- Incentives: Ensure that data scientists and statisticians in the public sector are appropriately remunerated [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3, wdr2021:p330:p4]. 

(2) Initiating data flows: 
- Data demand: Establish a culture of data use in ministries and among policy makers and legislators [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3, wdr2021:p330:p4]. 
- Incentives: Prioritize open data for development and use of common standards throughout the data life cycle [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3]. 
- Infrastructure policies: Establish a secure, integrated digital platform for storing and providing access to deidentified public intent data [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3]. 

(3) Optimizing the system: 
- Institutions: Charge an existing or new government unit with responsibility for overseeing and reporting on implementation of a national data strategy [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3]. 
- Incentives: Empower the NSO to take an active role in the national data system [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3]. 
- Policies: Define clear institutional mandates for the various government institutions [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3]. [wdr2021:p330:p4]

Integrating government
Government entities play a central role in the
national data system as the main producers of public intent data. To contribute to and sustain a strong
national data system, these entities must meet several objectives. They must address shortcomings in
the coverage, quality, and usability of public intent
data. They need to ensure the effective coordination
of public sector data producers and data exchanges
and the interoperability of data from various sources.
And they must make data available and accessible to
stakeholders across the system to promote use, reuse,
and repurposing (see figure 9.3).

raw_action.query: Figure 9.3 Steps to integrating the public sector into the national data system

raw_action.answer:
In Figure 9.3, the steps to integrating the public sector into the national data system are grouped as follows: 

(1) Establishing fundamentals: 
- Policies: Recognize the importance of an integrated national data system in a high-level strategic document [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3, wdr2021:p330:p4]. 
- Laws and regulations: Put in place robust data protection regulations [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3, wdr2021:p330:p4]. 
- Human capital and funding: Strengthen the technical capacity and financing of NSOs [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3, wdr2021:p330:p4]. 
- Institutions: Create technical units in ministries to strengthen administrative data and coordinate data [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3, wdr2021:p330:p4]. 
- Incentives: Ensure that data scientists and statisticians in the public sector are appropriately remunerated [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3, wdr2021:p330:p4]. 

(2) Initiating data flows: 
- Data demand: Establish a culture of data use in ministries and among policy makers and legislators [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3, wdr2021:p330:p4]. 
- Incentives: Prioritize open data for development and use of common standards throughout the data life cycle [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3]. 
- Infrastructure policies: Establish a secure, integrated digital platform for storing and providing access to deidentified public intent data [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3]. 

(3) Optimizing the system: 
- Institutions: Charge an existing or new government unit with responsibility for overseeing and reporting on implementation of a national data strategy [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3]. 
- Incentives: Empower the NSO to take an active role in the national data system [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3]. 
- Policies: Define clear institutional mandates for the various government institutions [wdr2021:p330:vis_figure_9_3].

question: Using Figure 3.5 (panels a and b), what share of Low-income, High-income, and Middle-income countries have Facebook, Google, and YouTube among the top 10 visited websites, and what is the global average daily time per user spent on Facebook.com, Google.com, Youtube.com, and Others?
answer: According to Figure 3.5, panel a, the share of countries where Facebook, Google, and YouTube are among the top 10 visited websites is 100% for Low-income countries, 94% for High-income countries, and 78% for Middle-income countries [wdr2021:p118:vis_figure_3_5]. The global average daily time spent per user on these websites is 17.42 minutes for Facebook.com, 13.12 minutes for Google.com, 13.04 minutes for Youtube.com, and 7.01 minutes for Others (average) [wdr2021:p118:vis_figure_3_5].

question: From Figure 5.3 (panels a and b), how did global Connected, Usage gap, and 3G Coverage gap shares shift between 2015 and 2018, and which regions represent the 2018 extremes in coverage gap and usage gap?
answer: Between 2015 and 2018, the global shares shifted as follows: the Connected population increased from 41% to 50%, the Usage gap rose from 37% to 42%, and the Coverage gap decreased from 21% to 8% [wdr2021:p181:vis_figure_5_3]. In 2018, the regional extremes for the coverage gap were North America (<1%) and Sub-Saharan Africa (29%) [wdr2021:p181:p0, wdr2021:p181:vis_figure_5_3]. For the usage gap, the extremes were South Asia (64%) and North America (15%) [wdr2021:p181:p0, wdr2021:p181:vis_figure_5_3]. [wdr2021:p181:p0]

results.text:
The reality is that the
actual expenditure on data services (known as average
revenue per user or ARPU) and the associated data consumption levels both fall well below these norms. In
fact, it is only when the cost per gigabyte of data drops
below 0.5 percent of gross national income (GNI) per
capita that data consumption reaches and eventually
exceeds the 1 gigabyte threshold (figure 5.8).
The amount of data that people can afford to consume is itself a function of the prices that operators
offer across different markets, as well as over time. In
India, rapid entry of mobile operators offering 4G service in 2016 boosted coverage from 4 percent in 2015
to 94 percent in 2018.

question: In Figure 7.2 (finalized digital platform antitrust cases as of January 2020), compare the total number of cases and top sectoral shares (%) between High-income countries (Panel a) and Middle-income countries (Panel b).
answer: As of January 2020, there were 62 finalized digital platform antitrust cases in high-income countries and 40 cases in middle-income countries [wdr2021:p250:vis_figure_7_2, wdr2021:p250:p6]. In high-income countries (Panel a), the top sectoral shares were Retail e-commerce (21%), followed by Online search and advertising (15%), Software and operating systems (15%), and Others (15%) [wdr2021:p250:vis_figure_7_2]. In middle-income countries (Panel b), the top sectoral shares were Passenger transport (35%), Retail e-commerce (23%), and Software and operating systems (18%) [wdr2021:p250:vis_figure_7_2]. results.text:
Enforcing antitrust laws
Antitrust investigations in the data economy are
not just a developed country phenomenon. Worldwide, as of January 2020 some 102 antitrust cases
across 16 different sectors on abuse of dominance,
anticompetitive agreements, and mergers had been
finalized.3 European antitrust authorities have finalized the most cases (33 percent), followed by authorities in East Asia and the Pacific (18 percent) and Latin
America (15 percent). The most active lower-middle-
income countries included the Arab Republic of
Egypt, India, and Kenya, with more cases still under
investigation in Indonesia, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe.

Antitrust investigations in the data economy are
not just a developed country phenomenon. Worldwide, as of January 2020 some 102 antitrust cases
across 16 different sectors on abuse of dominance,

America (15 percent). The most active lower-middle-
income countries included the Arab Republic of
Egypt, India, and Kenya, with more cases still under
investigation in Indonesia, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe.

question: Combining Figure 8.3 (page 293) and Figures 8.4 and 8.5 (page 296), compare Low-income vs High-income countries on: (1) established dedicated data governance entities and separate-agency share, (2) established data protection authorities, and (3) operational antitrust authorities.
answer: Based on the World Development Report 2021, the comparison between low-income and high-income countries is as follows: (1) Regarding data governance entities, no low-income countries have established a data governance entity [wdr2021:p293:vis_figure_8_3]. In contrast, 53% of high-income countries have established such entities [wdr2021:p293:vis_figure_8_3]. Among countries with an entity, 0% of lower-middle-income countries have a separate agency (all are part of another institution), whereas 56% of high-income countries have a separate data governance agency [wdr2021:p293:vis_figure_8_3]. (2) For data protection authorities, 3% of low-income countries have an established authority, compared to 81% of high-income countries [wdr2021:p296:vis_figure_8_4]. (3) Regarding operational antitrust authorities, 52% of low-income countries have an operational authority, compared to 75% of high-income countries [wdr2021:p296:vis_figure_8_5].

raw_action.answer: Based on the World Development Report 2021, the comparison between low-income and high-income countries is as follows: (1) Regarding data governance entities, no low-income countries have established a data governance entity [wdr2021:p293:vis_figure_8_3]. In contrast, 53% of high-income countries have established such entities [wdr2021:p293:vis_figure_8_3]. Among countries with an entity, 0% of lower-middle-income countries have a separate agency (all are part of another institution), whereas 56% of high-income countries have a separate data governance agency [wdr2021:p293:vis_figure_8_3]. (2) For data protection authorities, 3% of low-income countries have an established authority, compared to 81% of high-income countries [wdr2021:p296:vis_figure_8_4]. (3) Regarding operational antitrust authorities, 52% of low-income countries have an operational authority, compared to 75% of high-income countries [wdr2021:p296:vis_figure_8_5].

question: Combining Figure 8.2 (page 290) and Table 8.2 (page 292), identify all four thematic clusters of data governance functions, the specific bulleted sub-functions under each cluster, and the indicative actors/institutions assigned to each cluster.
answer: The four thematic clusters of data governance functions, their sub-functions, and indicative actors/institutions are as follows: 1) Strategic planning: Includes sub-functions 'Developing strategies and policies in line with the social contract for data' and 'Establishing institutional arrangements' [wdr2021:p292:vis_table_8_2]. Indicative actors include centralized data governance agencies/units (e.g., NSO, digital economy ministry), decentralized data governance units across government, CSOs, universities, and research institutions [wdr2021:p292:vis_table_8_2]. 2) Rule making and implementation: Includes sub-functions 'Legislating/regulating', 'Setting standards', and 'Providing clarification and guidance' [wdr2021:p292:vis_table_8_2]. Indicative actors include national legislatures, sector-specific regulators (telecom, banking/financial), industry associations, CSOs, Institutional Review Boards, and international institutions (sector-specific SSOs, international organizations like the World Bank, IMF, UN, WTO) [wdr2021:p292:vis_table_8_2]. 3) Compliance: Includes sub-functions 'Enforcing', 'Auditing', 'Arbitrating', and 'Remedying' [wdr2021:p292:vis_table_8_2]. Indicative actors include watchdogs and umpires such as data protection authorities, access to information agencies, antitrust authorities, consumer protection agencies, audit bodies, courts, ombudspersons, and CSIRTs [wdr2021:p292:vis_table_8_2]. 4) Learning and evidence: Includes sub-functions 'Engaging in backward-looking monitoring and evaluation' and 'Engaging in forward-looking learning and risk management' [wdr2021:p292:vis_table_8_2]. Indicative actors include the knowledge community, such as M&E units, CSOs, NGOs, multilateral development institutions, international development banks, academic institutions, think tanks, policy institutes, research institutions, news media, training bodies, and professional associations [wdr2021:p292:vis_table_8_2].

question: Combine the empirical data gap shown in Figure 5.6 (page 186) with the sequenced policies in Table 5.1 (page 197): how big is the 2018 mobile data consumption gap between Low-income / Sub-Saharan Africa and High-income economies, and what policies should countries in the 'Establishing fundamentals' and 'Initiating data flows' stages implement to close both coverage and usage/cost gaps?
answer:
In 2018, the mobile data consumption gap between High-income economies (7.1 GB per capita per month) and both Low-income countries (0.2 GB) and Sub-Saharan Africa (0.3 GB) was 6.9 GB and 6.8 GB, respectively [wdr2021:p186:vis_figure_5_6]. To address these gaps, countries should follow the sequenced policies in Table 5.1 [wdr2021:p197:vis_table_5_1]:

1. Establishing fundamentals: Countries should eliminate coverage gaps by reducing costs through wholesale and retail competition, infrastructure sharing, and well-crafted state support where necessary. They should also ensure adequate international bandwidth and create a competitive market for international gateways and internet service providers [wdr2021:p197:vis_table_5_1].

2. Initiating data flows: Countries should narrow usage gaps through digital literacy campaigns, investment in basic education, lowering taxes and import duties on low-end handsets, and supporting local handset manufacturing. Regarding connectivity, they should encourage the creation of the first domestic internet exchange point (IXP), facilitate participation by domestic players, allow additional IXPs to emerge, and encourage the caching of popular international content on local servers [wdr2021:p197:vis_table_5_1].

question: Combining Table 6.1 (page 227) and Table 7.1 (page 261), contrast the Global average regulatory score for Personal data safeguards vs E-commerce enablers, and explain how the Limited, Conditional, and Open transfers models trade off personal data protection, security goals, and regulatory costs.
answer: According to Table 6.1, the global average regulatory score for personal data safeguards is 44, while the global average score for e-commerce and e-transactions enablers is 73 [wdr2021:p227:vis_table_6_1]. Regarding the trade-offs between regulatory models for cross-border data transfers, the 'Limited transfers' model prioritizes cybersecurity and security concerns, resulting in higher regulatory costs and limited digital trade flows due to transfer approvals or localization requirements [wdr2021:p261:vis_table_7_1]. The 'Conditional transfers' model focuses on the protection of personal data, incurring medium regulatory costs and subjecting trade flows to regulatory conditions [wdr2021:p261:vis_table_7_1]. Finally, the 'Open transfers' model prioritizes business freedom, which minimizes regulatory costs and keeps digital trade flows largely open, though it provides few safeguards to boost trust [wdr2021:p261:vis_table_7_1].

raw_action.query: Table 6.1 page 227 Global average regulatory score Personal data safeguards Table 7.1 page 261 E-commerce enablers Limited Conditional Open transfers models

raw_action.answer: According to Table 6.1, the global average regulatory score for personal data safeguards is 44, while the global average score for e-commerce and e-transactions enablers is 73 [wdr2021:p227:vis_table_6_1]. Regarding the trade-offs between regulatory models for cross-border data transfers, the 'Limited transfers' model prioritizes cybersecurity and security concerns, resulting in higher regulatory costs and limited digital trade flows due to transfer approvals or localization requirements [wdr2021:p261:vis_table_7_1]. The 'Conditional transfers' model focuses on the protection of personal data, incurring medium regulatory costs and subjecting trade flows to regulatory conditions [wdr2021:p261:vis_table_7_1]. Finally, the 'Open transfers' model prioritizes business freedom, which minimizes regulatory costs and keeps digital trade flows largely open, though it provides few safeguards to boost trust [wdr2021:p261:vis_table_7_1].

question: On PDF page 120, what did the consumer behavior study reveal about default likelihood among customers arriving from a price comparison website versus customers directed via search engine ads, and what other types of non-attributable data are cited in that paragraph?
answer: On page 120, the consumer behavior study revealed that customers arriving from a price comparison website were roughly half as likely to default as those directed to the site via search engine ads [wdr2021:p120:p1]. Other types of non-attributable data cited in that paragraph include data on traffic, weather and climatic conditions, and network usage [wdr2021:p120:p1].

question: According to page 218, why can public sector adoption of privately developed automated decision-making systems hinder independent audits and trust, and what international ethical AI principles published in 2019 are highlighted?
answer: Public sector adoption of privately developed automated decision-making systems can hinder independent audits because the underlying algorithms may be protected by copyright or other intellectual property rights (IPRs), which restricts the ability to conduct independent third-party audits [wdr2021:p218:p0]. This lack of audits, combined with a lack of transparency and accountability, can impair public trust in institutional data processing and lead to unfair or discriminatory decisions [wdr2021:p218:p0]. The international ethical AI principles published in 2019, specifically those by the OECD and the Group of Twenty (G-20), highlight the necessity of ensuring transparency, explainability, and the inclusion of vulnerable or unrepresented groups in the design and implementation of AI systems [wdr2021:p218:p1].

Because of these challenges, as the uptake in
AI technologies and automated decision-making
systems increases in both the public and private
sectors, some principles for algorithmic regulation
are emerging at both the national and international
levels. Internationally, the focus has frequently been
on developing guiding principles based on data
ethics. For example, OECD and the Group of Twenty
(G-20) published two closely related sets of principles on ethical AI in 2019 that highlight the need to
ensure transparency, explainability, and inclusion of
unrepresented or vulnerable groups in the design

question: Based on page 252, why do multisided digital platforms create unique competition concerns regarding 'killer'/'zombie' acquisitions and bargaining power, and which three countries adopted complementary transaction-value merger notification thresholds?
answer: Multisided digital platforms create unique competition concerns regarding 'killer' or 'zombie' acquisitions because they can acquire potential competitors in complementary markets before those competitors become a threat, allowing the platform to shut them down or prevent their product development [wdr2021:p252:p2]. Additionally, the multisided nature of these platforms creates an imbalance in bargaining power between the platform and individuals or small suppliers (such as gig economy workers), which warrants policy attention [wdr2021:p252:p0]. The three countries that have adopted complementary transaction-value merger notification thresholds for digital markets are Austria, Germany, and Japan [wdr2021:p252:p4].

national data system

One way to increase the priority given to financing of data is to establish a target (percentage) for

view toward the resources needed to fully fund the
national statistical plan or be based on the spending of
peer countries that have achieved sufficient funding.

national development plan or through other means, it
arms data producers during later budget negotiations.

Development is at an intermediate level in areas
such as enabling reuse of public intent data, safeguarding both personal and nonpersonal data, protecting cybersecurity, and combating cybercrime. By
far the weakest area of performance of the surveyed
countries is enablers for private intent data. Overall,
the average scores of high-income countries are not
very high in absolute terms, warranting an advanced
(green) classification in table 6.1 in only one case. And
the score differential between high- and low-income
countries is relatively small (rarely more than 30
points). Both findings indicate the novel challenges
of developing a sound data governance legal framework and the significant progress all countries need
to make.

results.text:
Colocation
data centers offer companies multiple advantages,
including the physical space to store a growing
amount of data, the security associated with high
industry reliability standards (as they almost never
shut down), and easy internet access due to their
growing association with IXPs.93
Globally, some 3,700 data centers are connected
to the internet. 94 The disparities in data center penetration among country income levels are wide,
particularly when taking population differences into
account (figure 5.10). Although there are more than
three data centers per million inhabitants in North
America, the ratio is only 0.8 per million in South Asia
and Sub-Saharan Africa. In fact, there are more data
centers in the state of California than in all of Sub-
Saharan Africa.
